# A specialist company with room to grow

Leah Calder-Voss • Company planning note • 2 September 2026

KeplerOps is profitable. We have a working cash reserve and intend to fund the
next stage of growth from retained earnings and work we have contracted to do.
We remain privately held and founder-controlled, with minority ownership among
some early employees. There is no investor deadline requiring us to become a
different size by a particular year.

Our roughly twelve utility customers buy substantial organizational services.
Subscriptions and ongoing support provide most revenue. Implementation,
migrations, and scoped integration work provide the remainder. Several customer
contracts cover more than one department or site. Renewals, procurement exercises,
and expansion within customers are a substantial part of the commercial team's
work.

Over the next two years, I want us to add a few suitable customers and reduce
the share of engineering that must be repeated for each one. That requires
choices. A bespoke project can pay for useful capacity while consuming the
people who would otherwise make the product easier to maintain.

We should consider proposals against three questions:

- Does the work suit the product we intend to support?
- Can we meet the commitment while keeping our existing commitments?
- What will remain in our ordinary workload after the project closes?

The last question includes maintenance, support, documentation, and the work
an experienced person keeps doing after moving to a different role. Please
bring examples to your manager. An improvement need not be a new feature to
be worth funding.

We have 64 colleagues now. I would like this to remain somewhere people can
build a long career, including those who want to remain specialists. A good
next year should make the company more durable as well as larger.

# Working at KeplerOps

New-starter guide • Revised 7 September 2026

Welcome. Your buddy can help you find the people behind the names you encounter
in your first weeks. Ask questions as they arise; nobody expects the company
to become familiar all at once.

## What we make

FieldKest connects field submissions, maintenance packages, asset records, and
operational reports with the processes customers already use. We began as an
integration consultancy in 2016. The product grew out of repeatedly collecting
the same pieces of information so a customer could accept completed work.

We still earn our reputation through useful software and people who understand
its use. Our customers operate utilities. Their working day, procurement process,
and definition of a completed job may differ from ours.

## The people around you

| Function | Colleagues | Work |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| Product engineering | 22 | Product behaviour and customer compatibility |
| Support and implementation | 14 | Onboarding, cases, migration, and customer relationships |
| Platform and release | 7 | Build, release, service operation, and recoverability |
| Product management and quality | 8 | Priorities, testing, and acceptance |
| Commercial | 6 | Bids, renewals, and customer commitments |
| Leadership and business operations | 7 | Finance, people, purchasing, and running the company |

## Working together

Most locally based colleagues use Wednesday and Thursday as common office days.
Agree your own arrangements with your manager. Remote colleagues participate in
decisions and demonstrations; leave a useful written account when a conversation
produces a decision others need to know about.

Bring an example when it helps explain a question. You do not need a presentation
for every discussion. Release meetings normally have an agenda and an ending;
product discussions sometimes need a follow-up when an example raises another
question.

Your manager will discuss development with you. Specialist progression and
management are both available paths. Asking about a future role does not commit
you to applying for the next vacancy.

Social arrangements are optional. Some colleagues lunch together; others use
the break for errands or quiet time. Introductions across functions are part
of getting to know the work, and your buddy can arrange them.

# Rillhaven maintenance workshop

Preparation outline • Talia Mornac • Revised 9 September 2026

**Planned date:** Thursday, 24 September 2026

**Lead:** Talia Mornac. Maya Ranscombe will take questions about ongoing support.

Rillhaven's seasonal handover is complete. The workshop is an opportunity for
its staff to work through an example, discuss their experience, and offer product
feedback before the busiest part of the heating season.

## Proposed shape

1. Ask what each group wants to get from the session.
2. Work through one ordinary submission and its place in a maintenance package.
3. Let the customer explain which parts fit their own working day and which
   parts still take more effort than they should.
4. Discuss support questions with Maya.
5. Record product suggestions separately from commitments to deliver work.

The example should make clear who needs the result and what they do with it.
The introduction can be short. We should preserve time for questions rather
than trying to demonstrate every part of the product.

## After the rehearsal

The opening remains organized around the example. Maya's suggestion to explain
its intended audience earlier was useful and is included. Talia will lead the
presentation; Maya will support the discussion in the agreed part.

The workshop has not yet taken place. The follow-up will record questions,
agreed work, and suggestions once the customer has had the session.

# KeplerOps service review

Orren & Vale IT Services • 3 September 2026 • Review complete

The review covered the internal IT and backup-support work retained under the
current service arrangement. Completed routine maintenance was acknowledged,
and no further question remained against those completed items at the meeting.

KeplerOps' platform team continues to own product workloads. The managed-service
arrangement supports the agreed internal services; it does not transfer ownership
of the product platform to Orren & Vale.

Both parties agreed that account documentation should let a colleague pick up
an ordinary question without depending on one person's memory of earlier reviews.
Future scope changes will be described explicitly when proposed.

KeplerOps will suggest a suitable week for the next account review after its
planning calendar is settled. The next review has not yet been booked.

documents.name: k-company-history
documents.title: Ten years of KeplerOps
documents.text:
# Ten years of KeplerOps

Background for anniversary contributions • August 2026

Leah founded KeplerOps in 2016 to solve a repeated customer problem: field work
was complete, but the information needed to accept it was scattered among people
and systems. The first team worked from rented rooms and spent a good deal of
time visiting customers.

During 2018 and 2019, that work became FieldKest, a product we could support and
improve across customers. ARWC was among the utilities that helped us learn
what a substantial, repeated integration needed to do. Rowan joined in 2018;
Maya joined in 2019.

Remote working became established during 2020 and 2021. We also tried a simplified
self-service edition. Demand was limited: customers generally needed help with
their actual integrations. We wound down the edition while supporting existing
customers through the transition. Some of its design ideas remain fondly remembered.

In 2022 we moved to the current office and kept the hybrid model. The new space
made smaller conversations easier, although opinions about the old office remain
divided.

A substantial multi-site implementation finished in 2024, during a period when
we deliberately kept growth modest. The project photograph captures a result
worth being proud of. Other colleagues remember the routine work they kept
moving while that project received attention.

Hiring resumed selectively in 2025 and 2026. We have 64 colleagues and a clearer
framework for development. Newer employees now own work that used to depend on
someone knowing its whole history.

For the anniversary gathering, contributions from different years will sit
alongside this chronology. Please obtain the contributor's agreement before
sharing a personal account. The gathering is being arranged for November.

documents.title: Working with established utility customers
documents.text:
# Working with established utility customers

Support and implementation reference • September 2026

ARWC adopted FieldKest during 2018–2019 to improve the receipt of external field
and maintenance records. The early work reduced repeated collection of material
and helped us understand how a supported integration fits an established utility.

The relationship has matured. ARWC expects continuity when an individual colleague
is away. We support a product and agreed implementation work, rather than assuming
every request is a continuation of the original consultancy. Maya and Theo keep
much of the daily relationship moving, with Rowan and Clara contributing technical
expertise and commercial and procurement colleagues managing the contract.

ARWC is an important reference and renewal customer. A reference conversation
requires an agreed agenda and staff time. The customer should describe its own
experience in its own words.

Rillhaven District Heating uses a different supported interface and prepares
seasonal maintenance records ahead of increased heating demand. Its staff offer
constructive product feedback and appreciate practical workshops. A good idea
raised at a workshop is recorded as a suggestion until the appropriate work has
been agreed.

Our other utility customers have their own calendars, supported interfaces,
and habits. Keeping a useful account of those differences is part of the work.

# Rillhaven maintenance workshop — draft for rehearsal

Talia Mornac • 8 September 2026

The workshop is planned for Thursday, 24 September. Rillhaven's seasonal handover
is complete, and its staff have asked to work through an example and discuss
their experience.

I propose opening with one ordinary submission and explaining where it belongs
in a maintenance package. The customer should then have time to describe how
that fits their working day and what still takes unnecessary effort.

Maya can help with the questions about ongoing support. I would like to lead
the presentation myself. We should record product suggestions separately from
work we agree to deliver.

For tomorrow's rehearsal, I particularly want to check whether the example is
clear and whether enough time remains for questions. The introduction has already
been shortened; I do not think a longer product tour will help this audience.
